article.title: Lava Finds 24,650 Internet-Exposed Server BMCs Leaking Password Hashes Through a 2013 IPMI Flaw
article.summary: Security researchers found 24,650 of 36,872 internet-exposed server management interfaces leaking password hashes via a decades-old IPMI weakness, with one already targeted by a ransom note.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

More than 24,000 internet-exposed servers are leaking authentication password hashes from their Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) interfaces because of a weakness built into the IPMI 2.0 specification itself, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/). Researchers at cybersecurity and infrastructure startup Lava scanned the public internet for IPMI services exposed on UDP port 623 and found 36,872 internet-exposed hosts, of which 24,650 disclosed password-derived authentication material that could be used for offline password cracking, according to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html).

## What We Know

- The weakness is tracked as CVE-2013-4786, with a CVSS score of 7.5, according to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html).
- BMCs give administrators remote control over a server's hardware independent of its operating system, and researchers at Lava say recovered credentials may work across multiple management interfaces in the same environment, raising the stakes in shared infrastructure, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/).
- For at least a third of the affected hosts, researchers were able to find the correct password using dictionaries and the patterns on factory stickers for default credentials, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/). The Hacker News quotes security researcher Michael Katchinskiy putting a finer point on the same finding: "More than 30% of the returned hashes were associated with passwords that could be recovered using common wordlists and predictable factory chassis-sticker formats," according to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html).
- Separately, 2,340 instances used weak administrator passwords that matched public dictionaries, and 6,240 hosts accepted an empty username during authentication and were also protected only by weak passwords, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/).
- On a live exposure map reviewed by the outlet, the United States topped the list with 39% of the vulnerable servers, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/).
- Recovering an HPE factory password took about a day per captured authentication response on a single Apple M3 system, the researchers estimated, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/). Supermicro factory passwords, despite being uniquely assigned to each server, were recoverable in approximately one hour, according to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html).
- Researchers found an internet-exposed HPE iLO 4 login page displaying a ransom note demanding 0.3 BTC, evidence that at least some exposed interfaces have already drawn attacker attention, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/).
- In response to the disclosure, Supermicro said it will review or evaluate improvements to its default password policy for future hardware revisions, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) and [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html). Dell, in an advisory, called the issue "an inherent problem with the specification for IPMI v2.0" and said no patch is available, according to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html). HPE, however, gave the researchers only a standard auto-response with no follow-up from its security team, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/).
- Researchers recommend keeping IPMI and Redfish management interfaces off the public internet, rotating factory-set BMC passwords, restricting access to isolated management networks, and disabling legacy IPMI authentication, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/) and [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/24650-internet-exposed-bmcs-disclose.html).

## What We Don't Know

- Neither outlet names which organizations own the exposed servers, including the one displaying the HPE iLO 4 ransom note, so the scope of actual compromise beyond that single documented case is unclear.
- The Hacker News does not state which organization employs Michael Katchinskiy, the researcher it quotes, beyond identifying him as a "security researcher."
- Neither report specifies whether Dell's own IPMI implementations were part of the 36,872 hosts scanned or whether Dell's advisory was issued independently of this research.
